what_it_does: Modern processors automatically enter low-power sleep states (called C-states) when they have nothing to do; the deeper the sleep, the more power is saved, but the longer it takes to wake up and respond. BrokenSleep shows that this wake-up delay is large enough and consistent enough to be measured over a standard network connection: an attacker on the internet sends a request to a target server and measures how long the response takes; a slightly slower response reveals that the processor was in a deep sleep state, which reveals something about what the server was doing (or not doing) at that moment. The paper demonstrates two concrete attacks using this technique: a covert channel (a secret communication path between two processes that should not be able to talk to each other, by one process modulating its idle pattern and the other reading response times), and a side channel that can infer when a user is typing at a keyboard. The vulnerability exists on both Intel and ARM processors and requires no special hardware access or software bug.
